section.title: The Cheerful Giver
section.sectionRationale: Paul brings the appeal for the collection to its climax. He moves from the practical arrangements to the heart of the giver and the character of God. Using the image of sowing and reaping, he calls for glad, uncompelled generosity, and assures the Corinthians that God is able to supply everything they need so that they may abound in good works. The passage ends not with the gift but with the Giver, in a burst of praise for God's indescribable gift.
section.thesis: God loves a cheerful giver, and He is able to make all grace abound so that those who give generously will themselves be enriched in every way; for the God who supplies the seed multiplies the harvest, and the ministry of giving overflows in thanksgiving that rises to the God whose indescribable gift is Christ Himself.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the law of the harvest and the cheerful giver whom God loves; the God who supplies seed and multiplies righteousness so His people abound in every good work; and the overflow of thanksgiving to God, climaxing in praise for His indescribable gift.

verses.text: Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.
Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a {{hilaros|cheerful}} giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will {{perisseuo|abound}} in every good work.
As it is written: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.”

units.label: God supplies the seed
units.note: enriched in every way to be generous

verses.text: Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your store of seed and will increase the harvest of your righteousness.
You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will produce {{eucharistia|thanksgiving}} to God.
For this ministry of service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanksgiving to God.

Because of the proof this ministry provides, the saints will glorify God for your obedient confession of the gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all the others.
And their prayers for you will express their affection for you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you.
Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!

hilaros.gloss: Cheerful, glad, joyous; the source of the English word hilarious. Paul says that God loves a hilaros giver, one whose giving springs from a glad and willing heart rather than reluctance or coercion. The word points to a deep, joyful readiness that delights in the act of giving itself. God is not merely satisfied with the gift; He loves the giver whose generosity flows from joy.

perisseuo.gloss: To abound, to overflow, to have more than enough. Paul uses it to describe the abundance God supplies, not so that His people may hoard, but so that they may perisseuo, overflow, in every good work. The word carries the picture of a cup filled past the brim, a sufficiency from God that spills over into generosity toward others and finally into thanksgiving to God.

eucharistia.gloss: Thanksgiving, the giving of thanks, gratitude expressed. Paul says that the generosity of the Corinthians will produce eucharistia to God, and that the ministry overflows in many expressions of thanksgiving. The word shows that giving is not merely horizontal, meeting human need, but vertical, rising back to God as praise. Generosity completes its circuit only when it becomes worship in the mouths of those who are helped.

basic.context: Paul reaches the heart of his appeal for the collection. He sets out the law of the harvest, that sparing sowing brings a sparing crop and generous sowing a generous one, and he calls for giving that is glad and free, not grudging or forced, because God loves a cheerful giver. He then lifts the Corinthians' eyes to God, who supplies all they need, multiplies their harvest, and receives the thanksgiving that their generosity produces, ending in praise for His indescribable gift.
basic.hermeneutics: The sowing and reaping image must be read as gospel promise, not as a formula for getting rich. The harvest Paul has in view is a harvest of righteousness and thanksgiving to God, not guaranteed personal wealth. Read verses 6 to 11 in the light of verses 12 to 15, where the goal is that God is glorified and thanked.
basic.originalLanguages: God loves a hilaros giver, a cheerful, glad-hearted one, the word from which we get hilarious. He makes grace abound so that we perisseuo, overflow, in every good work. And generosity produces eucharistia, thanksgiving, to God, so that giving finally becomes worship.
basic.typology: The sowing and reaping of the field, and the God who gives seed to the sower and bread for food, draw on the whole biblical picture of harvest as a sign of God's provision. This points to Christ, the seed that fell into the ground and died to bear a great harvest, and to the indescribable gift in whom all God's blessings are given.
basic.christ: The passage ends with thanks to God for His indescribable gift, which is ultimately Christ Himself, God's own Son given for us. All Christian generosity is a response to that gift, a small imitation of the God who gave His best. Every act of giving is enfolded in the confession of the gospel of Christ that the saints glorify God for.
basic.god: God dominates these verses. He loves the cheerful giver, He is able to make all grace abound, He supplies and multiplies the seed, He increases the harvest of righteousness, and He receives the thanksgiving. The passage exalts a generous, all-sufficient God who gives so that His people may give, and who turns their generosity into worship of Himself.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 11 says the generous will be enriched. Luke 6 promises a good measure, pressed down and running over. Philippians 4 says God will supply every need according to His riches in Christ. John 3 declares that God so loved the world that He gave His only Son.
basic.oneStory: The Bible reveals a God who gives, supremely in the gift of His Son. The cheerful giver reflects that God, sowing generously because he has first received the indescribable gift. And the whole circuit of giving comes back to its source as thanksgiving, so that human generosity ends where it began, in the praise of the God who gave Christ for us.

context.literary:
Verses 6 to 15 are a single, carefully shaped sentence-chain about seed and harvest. They open with a proverb in verse 6, move to the individual in verse 7, widen to God in verse 8, confirm with Scripture in verse 9, and then unroll a long run of promises in verses 10 to 14 before ending in a short exclamation in verse 15. The rhythm moves from a short saying to a very long, overflowing statement, and then to a brief burst of praise, which seems to imitate the movement of grace itself.

The vocabulary of fullness holds the section together. Verse 8 contains the word 'all' five times in a row: all grace, all things, at all times, all that you need, every good work. Paul seems to be pressing the Corinthians against any lingering fear that giving will leave them short. The word for abundance and overflow keeps recurring, in verse 8, in verse 12, and in the ministry that is 'overflowing' in thanksgiving.

There is a clear circuit. God supplies seed in verse 10. The giver sows. The poor are relieved. And thanksgiving rises back to God in verses 11 to 13, where the giving reaches its true destination. The passage is built so that the last word returns to its source: 'thanks be to God.' This is a circular, not a linear movement. The gift comes down from God, passes through the church, and returns upward as praise.

A last literary point is that the passage reads as a gospel sermon on a very practical subject. Paul does not pause to argue about the amount. He is more concerned to make sure that the Corinthians see their gift as part of God's own movement toward the world.
context.historical:
Farming imagery came naturally to Paul's readers. Most people in the ancient Mediterranean lived close to the land. They knew that seed was precious, that a bad year might force a family to eat what they had meant to sow, and that sowing sparingly in the hope of saving grain was a real temptation. Paul's proverb in verse 6 works because the choice it describes was familiar.

The picture of the open hand on the field also has an Israelite background. The people were to leave the corners of the field for the poor, Leviticus 19:9-10, and the Lord had promised to bless the work of hands that gave freely, Deuteronomy 15:10. The poor in Judea were not an abstraction for Paul. Famine in the days of Claudius, Acts 11:28, and the cost of persecution had left many in need.

Verse 13 hints at the other side of the exchange. The Jerusalem believers will glorify God, and the 'obedient confession' of the Gentiles means that the Gentile churches have accepted the gospel and have not merely agreed with it. A Jewish church receiving help from Greeks would hear that the gospel had really reached the nations, as the prophets had promised, and their prayers for the Corinthians in verse 14 would knit two peoples together. Paul had already told the Romans that the Gentiles owed the Jews material help for the spiritual blessings they had shared, Romans 15:27.

The reference to 'ministry of service' in verse 12 uses language from temple worship, and the Jerusalem believers, many of whom still worshiped in the temple, would have heard it as a priestly word. An offering from the nations was therefore not only a relief gift but also a kind of worship in which Gentiles took part, and that makes the thanksgiving of verses 11 and 12 especially fitting.
context.canonical:
The chapter is full of Old Testament echoes. Verse 6 recalls the proverb that one gives freely and gains more, while another withholds and only becomes poor, Proverbs 11:24-25. Verse 7 is close to Deuteronomy 15:10, where the giver is told to give generously and not to let his heart be grieved. Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9, in which the righteous man scatters his gifts to the poor and his righteousness endures forever. Verse 10 draws on Isaiah 55:10, where God provides seed to sow and food to eat, and Hosea 10:12 speaks of sowing righteousness and reaping loving devotion.

Within Paul's own letters the harvest language reappears in Galatians 6:7-10, where those who sow to the Spirit reap eternal life and believers are urged to do good to everyone as they have opportunity, and in 1 Corinthians 3:6-9 where God gives the growth. Jesus taught the same measure in Luke 6:38, the good measure pressed down and running over, and in the words reported in Acts 20:35, that it is more blessed to give than to receive.

Verse 15 belongs to a small family of New Testament doxologies that end an argument with a burst of praise, as in Romans 11:33-36 and Romans 7:25. The word for gift in verse 15, dorea, is the term used for the gift of the Spirit in Acts 2:38 and for the gift of righteousness in Romans 5:17. Christians have long read it alongside John 3:16 and Romans 8:32, where the Father gives the Son and with Him all things. This chapter is therefore a bridge between the teaching on generosity and the gospel itself.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's first aim here is to remove fear. A church asked to give from limited means will naturally worry about what is left, and verses 8 to 10 answer that worry with a promise about God's supply. He does not promise that giving will make them rich. He promises that God is able to provide what they need so that they can keep on doing good. The promise answers the anxiety that would otherwise keep a hand closed.

His second aim is to lift the Corinthians' view of what they are doing. Handing money to a distant church is easy to see as a transaction or a duty. Paul shows them that it is part of a chain that ends in the praise of God, verses 11 to 13, and in the prayers of the saints, verse 14. They are taking part in worship across the churches.

His third aim is to speak to motive, because the difference between a gift and a levy lies in the heart. The statement that each should give what he has decided in his heart, verse 7, is a direct check on pressure. After pressing the Corinthians in chapter 8 and the first five verses of chapter 9, Paul takes care to say that he does not want a gift drawn out of them. He wants them to be moved.

First hearers would have taken from this that God is not in the business of taking from His people but of supplying them, and that their generosity was the means by which He answered the prayers of the poor in Judea.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The promises of verses 8 to 11 are given to a church that is giving to the needs of other believers in a specific project. They are not a promise attached to every financial transaction or to every act of giving. The text does not say that each coin returns as ten. The harvest in verse 10 is a harvest of righteousness, and the enrichment in verse 11 is for the purpose of being generous again.

The principles are prescriptive. Giving should be thought through and willing, verse 7. It should come from a settled decision of the heart and not from pressure, regret or the pull of the moment. It should be sown with the long view of a farmer, verse 6. And it should be accompanied by thanks to God, verse 11, since He has supplied both the seed and the sower.

Care is needed in applying the passage today. Sowing and reaping are real principles of how God often works, but they are not a contract. Believers who give generously and still suffer need are not failures of faith, as the Macedonian churches in the previous chapter show. And fundraisers who quote verse 7 to excuse pressure tactics, or verse 6 to promise financial return, are making the passage say what Paul does not. The more faithful reading is that generosity is a way of taking part in God's work and that He provides the means to continue.

debates.question: Does 'sow generously, reap generously' promise material wealth to the giver?

views.label: No, the harvest is righteousness and thanksgiving
views.case: The context explains the harvest. Verse 10 says God will increase the harvest of your righteousness, verse 11 says you will be enriched so as to be generous on every occasion, and verses 12 to 13 end in thanksgiving and glory to God. Each stage points toward good works and worship and not toward personal accumulation.

views.label: Yes, God returns material blessing to generous givers
views.case: Prosperity teaching reads verse 6 as a law of return and verse 8 as a promise of material sufficiency and more. It appeals to texts like Proverbs 11:25 and Luke 6:38 and treats giving as a kind of seed that produces financial increase.

views.label: A mixed view that allows God's provision without a guarantee
views.case: Some hold that God does often supply the generous with what they need, as verse 8 says, while denying that He promises surplus wealth or that any formula compels Him. Provision here means enough to keep giving.

debates.bearing: Verse 8 speaks of 'all that you need,' not all that you want, and verse 11 gives the purpose of any enrichment: more generosity. The apostle who wrote this letter was himself often in need, 11:27. The most faithful reading holds that God provides what is needed for good works and does not bind Himself to a scheme of financial return.

debates.question: Who is the 'He' who scattered gifts and whose righteousness endures forever in verse 9?

views.label: The righteous giver
views.case: Psalm 112 describes the man who fears the LORD, and verse 9 speaks of his scattering gifts to the poor. Paul applies it to the Corinthians as a picture of the person whose generosity shows a lasting righteousness.

views.label: God Himself
views.case: Verse 10 begins 'He who supplies seed,' and Paul may be thinking of God as the supreme scatterer of gifts, whose righteousness endures forever. Psalm 111, which comes just before, speaks of God's righteousness that endures forever in the same terms, and the two psalms were closely linked.

views.label: Both, since the giver reflects God
views.case: Psalm 112 is carefully written to show a righteous man whose character mirrors the LORD of Psalm 111. Paul can therefore apply it to the giver while knowing that the giver's generosity is derived from God's own.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is favored, the verse shows giving as a share in God's own character. The righteous person who gives to the poor is acting like the God who supplies, and the endurance of his righteousness is the mark of a life tied to Him.

debates.question: What is the 'indescribable gift' of verse 15?

views.label: Christ Himself
views.case: Paul often speaks of God's gift in the person and work of the Son, Romans 8:32 and Romans 5:15-17. After all that has been said about grace, this is the natural meaning, and the ancient church and most interpreters since have read it so.

views.label: The whole outworking of grace in the collection
views.case: Some take the gift as the unity, generosity and thanksgiving that the chapter describes, which is surpassing grace given to the Corinthians, verse 14.

debates.bearing: The two views are close, since the grace worked in the churches comes from Christ. The broader reading fits the immediate context, while the reading that sees Christ ties the section back to 8:9. Together they teach that all our giving is a response to a gift far greater than ours.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 6 contrasts sowing 'sparingly' and sowing 'generously.' The first word, pheidomenos, means 'holding back' or 'sparing,' a farmer clutching his seed. The second is literally 'with blessings,' ep' eulogiais, so that the generous sower sows blessings, and the harvest is also called blessing. The same word eulogia appeared in 9:5 for the 'generous gift,' and it is set against pleonexia, 'greed.' The thread is that a gift is a blessing given, and the opposite of blessing is grasping.

In verse 7 the verb translated 'decided' is prohaireomai, a deliberate choice made beforehand. Giving is a settled purpose and is neither an impulse nor an obligation. The two things Paul rules out are lype, 'grief' or 'sorrow,' translated 'regret,' and anagke, 'necessity' or 'compulsion.' Deuteronomy 15:10 speaks in the same terms of a giver whose heart is not grieved. Then comes hilaros, 'cheerful,' with the noun dotes, 'giver.' The Greek translation of Proverbs 22:8 says that God blesses a cheerful and giving man, and Paul's wording reflects that line. A related noun, hilarotes, appears in Romans 12:8, where acts of mercy are to be done with cheerfulness.

Verse 8 is a feast of the word 'all.' Pas, in several forms, occurs five times. The central noun is autarkeia, 'sufficiency,' often rendered 'contentment.' In Greek philosophy it described the self-sufficient person who needs nothing from outside. Paul gives it a new foundation. Sufficiency here is received, not achieved. God is dynatos, 'able,' and the word 'abound,' perisseuo, picks up the overflow vocabulary of chapter 8.

In verse 10 the verb for supply is epichoregeo, 'to furnish,' and the promise 'will supply' uses the same verb without its prefix, so that the One who now supplies is the One who will keep supplying. The picture of the sower and the bread closely follows the Greek of Isaiah 55:10. Paul says God will 'increase' the harvest of your 'righteousness,' dikaiosyne, the same word as in the Psalm quotation of verse 9. So righteousness here includes right dealing, mercy and justice toward the poor, as it does in Psalm 112:9.

Verse 11 uses haplotes again for 'generosity,' the single-hearted openness we met in 8:2. In verse 12 the 'ministry of service' is leitourgia diakonias, 'the liturgy of this service,' temple language, and the word 'supplying,' prosanaplerousa, means 'filling up what is lacking' with a prefix of extra. The supply of need is only half of the work. In verse 13 the 'proof' is dokime, the tested genuineness seen in 8:2 and 8:8, and homologia, 'confession,' is the public acknowledgment of the gospel. Finally in verse 15 the gift is dorea, a free and unearned gift, and the adjective 'indescribable' carries a negative prefix: something that cannot be fully told out.

typology.type: The sower and the seed, Isaiah 55:10-11
typology.fulfillment: God sends rain and snow so that the earth gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater, and His word accomplishes what He pleases. Paul uses that image of divine supply for the Corinthians, so that the God who provides seed also multiplies it. The pattern comes to its fullness in Christ, who is the sower of the word in the parable, Mark 4:3-9, and the grain that dies to bear much fruit, John 12:24. The type falls short in that Isaiah's harvest is food for the body, while the harvest in Christ is righteousness and everlasting life.

typology.type: The freewill offerings for the tabernacle, Exodus 35:5, 35:29
typology.fulfillment: Moses told the people that everyone with a willing heart should bring an offering, and they brought so much that he had to restrain them, Exodus 36:5-7. This is the first great picture of cheerful giving, an offering that flows from hearts the Lord has stirred. Paul's call in verse 7 to give what one has decided in the heart is its New Testament form. The escalation is that the offering now builds a living people and not a tent. The type falls short because the tabernacle gifts were gathered under Israel's covenant, whereas this giving crosses the line between Jew and Gentile.

typology.type: David and the people at the gathering for the temple, 1 Chronicles 29:6-17
typology.fulfillment: The leaders gave willingly, and the people rejoiced because they had given freely, and David prayed that everything comes from the LORD and that from His hand they had given. This matches the movement of 2 Corinthians 9, where gifts rise as thanksgiving to God. In Christ the true temple is His body, John 2:19-21, and the giving of the church builds it up. The correspondence breaks down in one place, for David gave to a building that would pass away, while the saints give to what will not.

typology.type: The Lord who gave His best, Genesis 22:12-16
typology.fulfillment: Abraham did not withhold his only son, and God's oath followed. The story points ahead to the God who did not withhold His own Son, Romans 8:32, whom Paul calls the indescribable gift in verse 15. Here the typology is partly by contrast, for Isaac was spared and a ram took his place, while Christ was not spared. The giving of Abraham teaches the shape of costly generosity, and the giving of the Father fulfills and exceeds it.

study.christ:
The passage ends with a single sentence of praise, and everything before it leads there. 'Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift' is not an afterthought. The whole of chapters 8 and 9 has been an argument that Christian giving is a reflection of one great gift, and in verse 15 Paul names the gift at last.

Most readers take the gift to be Christ, and the reasons are strong. In Romans 8:32 Paul says that the God who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all will freely give us all things with Him. In Romans 5:15 to 17 the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ overflow to many, and the same word dorea appears there. John 3:16 speaks of the God who so loved the world that He gave His only Son. If the word indescribable is to mean anything, it belongs to this gift, whose cost and depth no language can reach.

The earlier verses already point there. The giver in the passage is told that God loves a cheerful giver, and the one who gave most cheerfully was the Son. Hebrews 12:2 says that for the joy set before Him He endured the cross. The Lord did not give grudgingly or under compulsion. He laid down His life of His own accord, John 10:18, which is the pattern of verse 7.

There is also a link in the image of seed. In John 12:24 Jesus says that unless a grain of wheat falls to the ground and dies it remains alone, but if it dies it produces much fruit. He is the seed that was sown, and the harvest is the people He gathers. The multiplied harvest that Paul promises to the Corinthians is a small echo of the great harvest that Christ's death produced.

Paul's phrase 'obedient confession of the gospel of Christ' in verse 13 also matters. The saints in Jerusalem will glorify God because the generosity proves the Corinthians' confession is real. Christ is the content of that confession, the one in whom they believe and the one whom their generosity honors. A gift to a stranger in His name is a way of confessing Him.

One caution applies. The passage should not be read as if the Corinthians' giving earns anything from God or adds to Christ's work. Paul says that giving is itself a grace, and that its end is thanks. Christ's gift is complete, and every gift of ours is a response.
study.god:
This is the most God-centered paragraph of the whole collection appeal, and almost every verb in it has God as the one acting or as the one praised. He loves, He is able, He supplies, He multiplies, He increases, He is thanked, He is glorified. The human beings in the passage sow, give and pray, but each activity is set inside something God is doing.

First, God loves a cheerful giver. The verb is agapao, the love that chooses and delights. Paul does not say that God needs the money, and he does not say He will punish the grudging giver. He says that cheerfulness is something that pleases Him, because it resembles what He is. A cheerful giver is a person who has come to share the Father's own spirit. That also makes sense of Proverbs 22:8 in the Greek translation, which says that God blesses a cheerful and giving man.

Second, God is able. The word dynatos in verse 8 declares power, and the power is directed at grace: 'able to make all grace abound.' The God of this passage is not stingy and not stretched. He is also generous toward the Corinthians themselves, so that they can have all they need. This is the answer to the fear that giving will bring loss.

Third, God is the source of everything that is given. The seed in verse 10 is from Him, the sower is supplied by Him, and the bread for food is His, as Isaiah 55:10 had said. David had prayed in 1 Chronicles 29:14 that everything comes from the LORD and that from His own hand they had given to Him. A person who gives is passing along what was first given.

Fourth, God is righteous, and His righteousness endures forever, verse 9. The Psalm text sets the ongoing, steady character of the Lord against the passing character of material things. A giver's righteousness has permanence because it shares in His.

Fifth, God is the one to whom all thanksgiving is directed. The movement of the passage is toward praise, and its last words are 'thanks be to God.' He is not a merely useful provider. He is the end of every road in the chapter. For worship, this means that the proper climate of giving is gratitude and joy, and that a church should hold its offerings, in the most ordinary sense, as an act in which God is thanked for being the God who gives.

crossReferences.note: One gives freely and gains more, another withholds and only becomes poor, and the generous soul will prosper. This is the proverb tradition behind verse 6. Paul takes it up but turns the result toward righteousness and thanksgiving, as the verses that follow make plain.

Give generously to the poor brother and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so, and the LORD will bless you in all your work. The warning about a grieved heart is the Old Testament form of 'not out of regret,' and the promise of blessing is the background to verse 8.

The quotation in verse 9. The man who fears the LORD has scattered gifts to the poor and his righteousness endures forever. Reading the whole psalm shows a person whose generosity grows out of trust, with a heart steadfast and unafraid of bad news.

Rain and snow come down to give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, and God's word accomplishes what He pleases. Verse 10 echoes the wording closely, and it helps the reader see that the harvest in view is the fruit of God's own purpose.

Whatever a man sows he will reap, and believers are not to grow weary in doing good. Paul uses the same sowing language of the Spirit in another letter, and it shows that the principle in 2 Corinthians 9:6 belongs to his wider teaching on the fruit of a life lived for others.

Jesus promises that a good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, will be poured into the giver's lap. It is the saying behind much teaching on generosity and, read with Paul's context, it speaks of the generosity of God and not of a financial scheme.

Paul says he does not seek the gift but the fruit that may be credited to the givers' account, that their gifts are a fragrant offering pleasing to God, and that God will supply all their needs. It is a close companion to verse 8 and shows the same logic of an offering received by God and answered by God.

David asks who he is that he can give so generously, since everything comes from the LORD. It is the clearest Old Testament statement that giving returns to God what is already His, and it frames the thanksgiving of verses 11 to 13.

The God who did not spare His own Son but gave Him for us will also give us all things with Him. This verse supplies the argument behind verse 15: if the Father has given the greatest gift, no lesser provision will be withheld.

Paul recalls the words of the Lord Jesus, that it is more blessed to give than to receive. The saying shows that the joy of verse 7 is not Paul's invention. It goes back to Jesus and describes what the giver discovers.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is a story of seed and harvest from the first page. On the third day of creation God calls the earth to bring forth plants bearing seed, Genesis 1:11-12, and He gives the man and woman every seed-bearing plant for food, Genesis 1:29. The garden is a place of provision, and the fall interrupts it with thorns and toil, Genesis 3:17-19. From then on the harvest is both a sign of God's mercy and a place where the curse is felt.

God's covenant with Noah promises that seedtime and harvest will not cease, Genesis 8:22, and Israel is brought into a land of grain and wine and asked to remember the poor at harvest. The prophets picture the restoration as a sowing: Hosea 2:21-23 says that God will answer the earth and the earth will answer the grain, and Isaiah 55 and Amos 9:13 describe an overflowing harvest. The land's fruit is always a gift.

Against that background Paul's teaching is the harvest of the gospel. Jesus describes Himself as the grain that dies, John 12:24, and sends out His disciples into a harvest that is plentiful, Matthew 9:37-38. The Corinthians' gift is one grain from that field. It is a harvest of righteousness, produced by God and returned to Him in thanks. The Gentiles' giving to Jews also works toward a new unity, where those once far off are brought near, Ephesians 2:13, and where the nations bring gifts to Zion as Isaiah foretold.

The story closes with a harvest too. Revelation 14:14-16 shows the harvest of the earth, and Revelation 22:2 gives a tree of life bearing fruit every month beside the river of the water of life. The scarcity that began in Genesis 3 is undone. Nobody sows in tears there, Psalm 126:5-6, and nobody wonders whether giving will leave them short. The people who have sown in this world with open hands will see what their sowing became. The last word of the story is the one Paul reaches at the end of this chapter: thanks, because the God who gave His Son has given everything else in Him, and because the giving that began in Him ends in Him.

quiz.q: What kind of giver does God love, according to verse 7?

options.text: A cheerful giver, who gives from a glad heart, not from regret or compulsion.
options.note: God loves the hilaros, cheerful, giver whose generosity springs from joy.

options.text: A giver who gives the largest possible amount.
options.note: The heart behind the gift, not its size, is Paul's point.

options.text: A giver who gives only when he feels obligated.
options.note: Paul excludes giving out of compulsion; God loves cheerful giving.

options.text: A giver who lets everyone see how much he gives.
options.note: The concern is the gladness of the heart, not public display.

quiz.q: Why does God make all grace abound to His people?

options.text: So that, having all they need, they may abound in every good work.
options.note: Verse 8 says the abundance is for overflowing in good works, not hoarding.

options.text: So that they may become personally wealthy.
options.note: The aim is generosity and good works, not personal riches.

options.text: So that they will never face any hardship.
options.note: God supplies sufficiency for good works, not a life free of hardship.

options.text: So that they can stop depending on Him.
options.note: His supply deepens dependence and generosity, not independence.

quiz.q: What does the Corinthians' generosity ultimately produce?

options.text: Thanksgiving and glory to God from those whose needs are met.
options.note: Verses 11 to 13 show generosity overflowing in thanksgiving to God.

options.text: A reputation that makes the Corinthians famous.
options.note: The result is praise to God, not fame for the givers.

options.text: A debt that the recipients must repay.
options.note: It produces prayer and thanks, not obligation to repay.

options.text: Nothing beyond the meeting of physical needs.
options.note: It does more than meet needs; it rises to God as worship.

quiz.q: What is the indescribable gift Paul praises God for in verse 15?

options.text: Christ Himself, God's own Son, the fountain of every grace.
options.note: The doxology lands on God's supreme gift of Christ.

options.text: The money collected for the Jerusalem church.
options.note: The collection flows from the gift, but the gift itself is far greater.

options.text: The eloquence God gave Paul to write the letter.
options.note: The gift is God's own, not Paul's ability.

options.text: A special reward promised to generous givers.
options.note: The gift is Christ, given to all, not a payment for giving.

questions: God loves a cheerful giver, not merely a giver. How does the state of your heart, and not just the size of your gift, matter to God?
Paul roots giving in the promise that God is able to make all grace abound. Where do fears about not having enough keep you from generosity, and how does this promise speak to them?
The passage warns against giving out of regret or compulsion. What would need to change for your giving to become glad and free rather than pressured?
Generosity meeting need overflows in thanksgiving to God. How does it reframe your giving to see it as producing worship, not just transferring resources?
The chapter ends with thanks for God's indescribable gift in Christ. How does dwelling on the gift you have received in Jesus fuel your own generosity?

translationNotes.note: Cheerful renders hilaros, the source of the English word hilarious, denoting a glad, joyous readiness; the clause echoes the Septuagint addition at Proverbs 22:8.
The quotation is from Psalm 112:9; set as poetry in the source, it is rendered here as prose within the verse, with quotation marks retained.
Indescribable renders a word meaning inexpressible or beyond words; the gift is most naturally understood as Christ Himself, the source of every grace named in the chapter.
